1:
Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter into two revelations, a vision of resurrection and an acted sign of reunion. Clarke summarises the first as a scattered people's hopeless condition, reversed against all probability, then reads a transition to a larger blessedness. Ellicott places the scene: the word for the plain carries the article and is probably the one where earlier visions were given, and he would punctuate so the bones become a fresh statement rather than a description. They lay strewn thickly rather than heaped, and a mind long occupied with devastating campaigns would come by such images naturally.

Henry insists the thing shown is beyond nature, since there is no road back from deprivation to possession, so only a word from God could suggest it; he reports the argument that the vision could not confirm anything unless the general resurrection it borrows were itself certain. Wesley finds three resurrections in the figure: souls out of the death of sin, a church out of affliction into liberty, the body at the last day. Ellicott takes the dryness for a measure of time, showing how long life had gone and how remote its return.

The question to the prophet is deliberate. Ellicott says it presses the human impossibility of what omnipotence is about to do at once, the lesson needed by hearers who had disbelieved the threats and now disbelieved the promises; the answer leaving the matter with God comes from a man who sees the impossibility and suspects a reason behind the asking. Gill turns it into a fruitless search for means, Clarke into a plain question of possibility. Ellicott notes that prophesying here is speaking on God's behalf and carries no idea of prediction, while Clarke makes it an address to miserable countrymen whose case is not hopeless.

The word for what enters them is ambiguous. Clarke says the term covers soul, breath, wind and sometimes the Spirit of God, and takes soul here; Ellicott points out that one Hebrew word carries breath, wind and spirit alike, that Greek doubles two of the three, and that only context decides. The rebuilding is followed step by step. Gill has sinews first to join, then flesh to cover and give motion; Clarke counts six stages from bones through ligaments, muscle and skin to bodies complete but soulless, then the entering breath, comparing the first man before he received his own principle of life. Ellicott makes the two stages an evident echo of that creation account, form first and life after.

Wesley dwells on the noise. There was a rattling as the bones moved and a commotion large enough to declare a presence, then a gliding together, each bone finding its own; of all those slain not one bone was missing, none went astray, none took a wrong place, which he offers as a picture of scattered atoms reassembled at the last. Gill marks the two prophesyings as distinct, the first leaving the work unfinished for want of breath. Clarke reads the summons to the four winds as a call to souls from every quarter; Ellicott observes that the dead are specifically the slain, which is where the likeness to the nation lies.

The interpretation removes the guesswork, Ellicott says, whatever else the imagery might have borne, and he corrects an obscure clause to read simply that as for us, we are cut off. Wesley matches hopelessness to hopelessness; Clarke equates bones with condition and revival with return, and calls the graves a pointed allusion to a resurrection the people already believed. Ellicott explains the change of scene, since bones must lie open to be seen while the dead belong in graves. On the Spirit, Clarke distinguishes the soul already given from the Spirit that makes men obedient, Gill lists what it works, and Ellicott ties the moral resurrection to the national as both condition and later fruit.
15:
Henry states the second sign's promise as brotherly union, ending feuds that ran from the first revolt, and reads through it to a wider peace under the Messiah. Ellicott is careful about the object: these are not the rods of the earlier trial of the tribes, whatever the prophet had in mind, since the word differs and means simply a piece of wood, the two doubtless shaped to look like one when held together. Gill offers tablet, board or plank, reports versions rendering it a rod, and takes it for an emblem of a kingdom; Wesley calls it a writing tablet or tally.

The labels are read as political arithmetic. Clarke sets out the composition of the two states, one of two tribes with the Levites and the other of all that went off in the schism, and notes that some individuals rejoined the south without altering the division. Ellicott explains why neither name could stand alone, since each kingdom held associates that had to be named with it. Wesley identifies the companions on each side, and he and Clarke both note that the northern kingdom is named from its chief tribe because its first king came from it. Ellicott adds the contrast that carries the point: the human hand that made and kept the division against the hand in which the pieces become one.

Ellicott watches the staging. The sign was not only performed in sight of the people; the joined wood was to stay in the prophet's hand while the promise was explained, and that promise largely repeats what two earlier chapters had said.

On how far the promise reached, the commentators separate. Clarke observes that the distinction between the kingdoms did disappear after the return, but denies that a single king ever followed politically, so the union spoken of belongs to another time and kingdom. Gill and Wesley both take the one king for the Messiah directly, Wesley reading the earlier united reign as a type and finding the peace-maker in the name of the king who followed it. Ellicott resists in part: the gathering from among the nations is the first step, but it was fulfilled to a remnant only, any larger fulfilment being prevented by the people's own sins, God doing all their disobedience left possible.

The name of the promised king is read the same way by everyone here. Gill reports the Jewish commentators who make it the Messiah, of whom the older king was a type, and takes the title of servant so; Clarke refers the identification to an earlier chapter; Ellicott notes the figure described personally as the one king and shepherd; Wesley makes him the chief shepherd under whom others feed the flock by commission.

The closing promises turn on one word. Ellicott points out how heavily the text leans on for ever, applying it to the land, the kingship, the sanctuary and the covenant in turn, and says these are the promises later Scripture takes up of an everlasting reign and an indwelling in the believer. Wesley reads the sanctuary as a spiritual temple never abolished on earth and consummated in heaven; Gill takes the covenant of peace for the covenant of grace with reconciliation as its principal article, and the tabernacle for an indwelling that makes each of them a temple. Clarke identifies the tabernacle with Christ himself; Ellicott traces the promise from a shadow in the rebuilt temple to its reality in an incarnation the Greek describes with that same verb. On the increase promised, Ellicott extends the patriarch's fatherhood to all who walk in his faith, whatever their descent; Gill closes on the watching nations, to observe what holiness God works in a people set apart.
